column3: Repeats the Book portrait and the exact paired titles messenger and prophet for Ishmael.
Shows Noah's public commission as a sent messenger and clear warner.
Repeats the Book portrait and prophet designation for Idris, closely paralleling Moses's presentation.
Places prophethood among Abraham's divinely granted family, immediately before Moses's portrait.
Joins messenger with the prophetic line, defining its culminating continuity in Muhammad.
Uses the same Book-remembrance and prophet-portrait form for Abraham.
Names God's purified servants, directly clarifying Moses's description as mukhlas.
Sets individual prophethood within a recurrent history of sent prophets.
Combines servanthood, a received Book, and prophethood in Jesus's self-description.
Defines sincere religion as exclusive attachment to God, illuminating purified devotion.
Links the revealed Book to worship rendered sincerely and exclusively for God.
Has Moses and Aaron identify themselves together as messengers of the Lord of all worlds.
Records Moses's reception of the Book and Criterion as guidance.
Continues Moses's account with Aaron granted as a prophet and brotherly support.
Voices worship of God with religion made exclusively His.
Again distinguishes God's purified servants, reinforcing the consecration in the focus.
Names Moses as recipient of the Book for his people's guidance.
Calls Isaac a prophet, extending the succession of named prophetic figures.
Describes a messenger who recites signs, purifies, and teaches the Book and wisdom.
Presents earlier messengers sent to their peoples with clear proofs.
Affirms that God fulfills His promise to His messengers.
Recalls Moses as vindicated and honored in God's presence.
Immediately continues Moses's account with God's call and intimate nearness.
Names Moses among the prophets whose revelations share one divine source.
Identifies Moses's Book as a prior guide and mercy.
Completes Ishmael's adjacent prophet portrait through his faithful worship and household leadership.
States the pattern of sending a messenger who recites divine signs before judgment.
Explains divine communication, including revelation through a commissioned messenger.
Connects Noah and Abraham's line with the placement of prophethood and the Book.
Has Moses explicitly declare himself a messenger from the Lord of all worlds before Pharaoh.
Pairs Moses's received Book with Aaron appointed as his supporting minister.
Associates prophets with the Book sent in truth for human guidance and judgment.
Reaffirms Moses's received Book as guidance for the Children of Israel.
Summarizes the favored prophets, including the lines of Noah, Abraham, and Israel, in the same passage sequence.
Describes the messenger's work of recitation, purification, and teaching the Book.
Affirms Jonah's enduring identity among the sent messengers.
Affirms Elijah's identity among the sent messengers.
Affirms Lot's identity among the sent messengers.
Addresses resistance to God's sending a human messenger with guidance.
Combines a messenger from God with recitation of purified scriptures.
Distinguishes God's communications from the messenger charged to convey them.
Shows Moses and Aaron jointly guided on the straight path after their deliverance.
Begins the same Book-remembrance sequence with Mary, establishing its recurring portrait form.
Portrays Abraham as grateful, chosen, and guided, paralleling the divine election behind Moses's consecration.
Confirms that the messengers have conveyed their Lord's messages.
Pairs remembrance of David with his identity as God's servant and persistent return.
Identifies Noah as a trustworthy messenger, adding a moral quality of prophetic transmission.
Identifies Hud as a trustworthy messenger amid his call to his people.
Identifies Salih as a trustworthy messenger in his people's warning narrative.
Identifies Lot as a trustworthy messenger within his public mission.
Identifies Shu'ayb as a trustworthy messenger, extending the shared prophetic ethic.
Links the later messenger to Abraham's upright, non-idolatrous devotion.
Uses the same purification root for chosen servants whose orientation is made exclusive through remembrance of the Hereafter.
Places the Prophet within God's established pattern for earlier prophets.
States sincere, exclusive devotion to God, directly paralleling Moses's purified orientation.
Attributes piety and divinely given purity to John within the same succession of prophetic portraits.
